rationale: A wins because it knows the difference between a pitchable angle and a trap door. Its line, “The store that costs more to build is the one Warby says pays off,” correctly makes the money story conditional and keeps the exam-revenue hole visible; B’s “Warby Parker says it’s profitable — but won’t say how much comes from eye exams” turns a missing breakout into a sharper accusation than the facts support. B is useful, but A is cleaner, more disciplined, and less tempted by its own headline.
gaps_in_A: The trend angle “A DTC eyewear brand is quietly becoming a place you get your eyes checked” still needs outside pattern proof; A admits this, but without comparables it is one-company evidence wearing a trend jacket.

“Decay: 24hr” on the competitive optometrist angle is a little too severe; the announcement peg fades fast, but the incumbent-moat framing could support a slower trade feature if Warby supplies numbers.
The pharmacy angle is correctly flagged as thin, but “pharmacy counter” adds a consumer image not present in the facts; keep it as pharmacy-chain distribution until the format is known.
gaps_in_B: “Warby Parker says it’s profitable — but won’t say how much comes from eye exams” overstates the disclosure story. The facts say exam-revenue contribution is not broken out; they do not say Warby was asked, refused, or highlighted profitability and exams “in the same breath.”
“CVS-MinuteClinic-style trend” smuggles in a specific comparator not supplied by the update. It may be fair background, but it is not grounded in the provided facts.

“testing whether a pharmacy aisle sells glasses better than its own stores” invents the test. The update says Warby is piloting a pharmacy-chain partnership, not that it is benchmarking pharmacy sales against owned stores.
“Decay: month” for the retail-health angle is generous. With only one company announcement and no outside trend evidence, that is a week-long feature peg, not a month-long story.
